title: Error Handling
description: Typed errors, discriminated error unions, the never type, and patterns that make failures explicit.

challenges.title: Why catch gives you unknown
challenges.description:
In strict TypeScript, what type is `err` in a catch block, and what must you do before calling `err.message`?

  try { riskyOp() } catch (err) { console.log(err.message) }
challenges.whyMatters: Untyped catch blocks are the most common source of runtime crashes in TypeScript software engineering scripts. Understanding this prevents silent failures in production.
hints: err is unknown — you must narrow it before accessing properties

choices.label: err is Error — .message is always safe
err is unknown — you must narrow with instanceof Error before using .message
err is any — anything goes
err is string — it's always the error message

challenges.title: Custom error classes
challenges.whyMatters: Custom error classes let you distinguish between a timeout, a DNS failure, and an auth error in your catch block — essential for intelligent retry logic.
hints: instanceof only works with class instances, not plain objects or type aliases

choices.label: A)  const NetworkError = { message: 'network failed' }
B)  type NetworkError = { message: string }
C)  class NetworkError extends Error { ... }
D)  const NetworkError = (msg: string) => new Error(msg)

challenges.title: Write a typed error hierarchy
challenges.description:
Create a typed error hierarchy:

- `AppError` — base class extending Error, adds `code: string` property
- `NetworkError` extends AppError — adds `statusCode: number`
- `ConfigError` extends AppError — adds `field: string`

Then write `handleError(err: unknown): string` that:
- If it's a NetworkError: returns `"Network [statusCode]: message"`
- If it's a ConfigError: returns `"Config error on field 'field': message"`
- If it's an AppError: returns `"App error [code]: message"`
- If it's a plain Error: returns `"Error: message"`
- Otherwise: returns `"Unknown error"`
challenges.whyMatters: This is the error handling pattern used in every robust software engineering tool — a hierarchy you can catch broadly or narrowly depending on what you need to do.
hints: Check most specific type first: NetworkError before AppError
instanceof checks go from most specific to least specific
Set this.name = 'NetworkError' etc. in each constructor for better stack traces

challenges.title: The never type
challenges.whyMatters: Exhaustive checks mean adding a new Status value forces a compile error everywhere the switch is used — no silent unhandled cases in your monitoring code.
hints: never is the type of something that can never occur — if the default is reached, something went wrong

choices.label: It crashes at runtime if an unknown status is passed
It causes a compile error if any Status value is not handled in the switch
It returns undefined for unknown values
It is just a convention — no actual enforcement

challenges.title: Discriminated union errors
challenges.whyMatters: Discriminated unions make error handling exhaustive and self-documenting — each error shape has exactly the fields it needs, no undefined optional fields.
hints: The discriminant is the shared literal property — 'kind' in this case

choices.label: The kind property is a literal type shared across all variants — narrowing on it gives you the exact shape
It is a class hierarchy in disguise
Optional fields would be just as type-safe
There is no practical difference from a single Error class

challenges.title: Write an error discriminated union handler
challenges.description:
Define a discriminated union type `ServiceError`:
- `{ kind: 'network'; statusCode: number; url: string }`
- `{ kind: 'timeout'; url: string; durationMs: number }`
- `{ kind: 'config'; field: string; reason: string }`

Write `formatError(err: ServiceError): string` that returns:
- network: `"HTTP statusCode at url"`
- timeout: `"Timeout after durationMsms at url"`
- config: `"Invalid config field 'field': reason"`

Write `shouldRetry(err: ServiceError): boolean`:
- network with statusCode >= 500: true
- timeout: true
- everything else: false

Make the switch exhaustive with a never guard.
challenges.whyMatters: shouldRetry is a real function you'd write in any resilient software engineering tool — the discriminated union makes it impossible to forget a case.
hints: For the never guard in default: const _: never = err; throw new Error('unhandled')
statusCode >= 500 check goes inside the 'network' case

challenges.title: Error boundaries with Result
challenges.description:
Which of these patterns best prevents unhandled exceptions from propagating in a CLI tool?

  A)  Wrap everything in try/catch at the top level
  B)  Use Result<T, E> return types so errors are part of the function signature
  C)  Use process.on('uncaughtException') to catch everything
  D)  Never throw — return undefined on failure
challenges.whyMatters: Result types make error paths visible at the call site — callers can't ignore failures the way they can with thrown exceptions.
hints: Think about what the type system can enforce vs what it can't

choices.label: A)  Wrap everything in try/catch at the top level
B)  Use Result<T, E> return types so errors are part of the function signature
C)  Use process.on('uncaughtException') to catch everything
D)  Never throw — return undefined on failure

challenges.title: Build a safe async wrapper
challenges.description:
Write a generic function `tryCatch<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<Result<T>>`

Where Result<T> is:
- `{ ok: true; value: T }` on success
- `{ ok: false; error: string }` on failure

It should never throw — always return a Result.

Then write `runAll<T>(tasks: Array<() => Promise<T>>): Promise<Result<T>[]>` that runs all tasks in parallel and returns all results (never rejects).

Finally write `countResults<T>(results: Result<T>[]): { passed: number; failed: number }`.
challenges.whyMatters: tryCatch + runAll is the pattern behind every parallel health checker, batch processor, and multi-service status tool you'd write.
hints: In tryCatch, use try/catch inside an async function, return { ok: true, value } or { ok: false, error: String(e) }
runAll maps each task through tryCatch, then Promise.all
